source.title: Theoretical Characterization of the Generalization Performance of Overfitted Meta-Learning
source.authors: Pei-Zhong Ju; Yitao Liang; N. Shroff

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: It analyzes feature-count-dependent generalization for overfitted MAML using a linear Gaussian model and reports a neural-network width experiment. These are different settings and measures from the original double-descent studies, but they bear directly on capacity-related generalization.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own feature-count sweeps and a neural-network width experiment. Results cited from other papers are not included as rows. It does not sweep epochs or training-sample counts. Figure 1 values are reported only in plots; the text describes their trends.
record.test_reason: The study applies double descent to a new setting, overfitted min-ℓ2-norm MAML meta-learning in a Gaussian linear model plus a small two-layer MNIST net. It reports its own simulated and theoretical model-error curves versus feature count p past the interpolation point p=mnv, and their dependence on noise σ and task diversity ν. These bear on V4, the second descent in a non-deep model class, and on V6, noise/variance dependence. It is not a reproduction of the original recipe.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that the overfitted min-ℓ2-norm MAML solution can be benign: its model error descends in p past p=mnv. The descent is easier to see under large noise and task diversity, and with small noise/diversity it has a floor whose value and location rise with ν and σ. Unlike single-task regression, descent occurs even at zero noise if task diversity is nonzero. With large σ, ν and small ||w0||, the overfitted solution can beat the underparameterized one. A small MNIST net shows an overall decreasing test error with width, with floors.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes min ℓ2-norm overfitted MAML in a Gaussian linear meta-learning setup and adds a two-layer MNIST experiment; it is not a reproduction of the original double-descent setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported feature-count curve changes with training-task noise σ and task diversity ν; low values are associated with descent floors, while larger values make descent easier to observe.
record.problems: The main feature-count evidence is for model error and theoretical bounds rather than directly measured test error. Figure 1 values are not given numerically in the text. The neural-network experiment has 30 runs and a qualitative figure description, but does not report a fitted-size threshold or a full double-descent curve.

untested.parts: No peak near the size that just fits the training set: the MNIST width sweep (40–500) appears to be all interpolating, so only the post-threshold fall is visible.
Sample count is not swept near the interpolation threshold.
The peak at p=mnv is not characterized; analysis is restricted to p>mnv aside from the p=s point.
No effective-complexity predictor of peak location.
Multiple or split peaks are not studied. Removal of the peak under optimally tuned regularization is not tested.

missing.what: Figure 2: simulated model error versus the theoretical bound (Theorem 1/Eq. 9) for each of the five (ν,σ) settings, showing close match; the constants C1–C4 were hand-calibrated.
Underparameterized p=s=1 model-error approximation (ν²/m + σ²/m + …), used as the comparison against overfitted solutions.

record.verdict_notes: The main measure is model error, which Lemma 1 links monotonically to test error. Fig. 1 values are figure-only. The interpolation threshold here is p=mnv=30. The study does not describe a peak there, only post-threshold behaviour. I set the tranche to T3 (new meta-learning setting) rather than the reader's T2. I split the reader's single V4 'supports' by noise/diversity regime, because the low-noise curves rise again after a floor. V1 gets no verdict: r7's width range appears entirely past interpolation, so the peak is untested rather than limited.

versions.untested_parts: The MNIST experiment varies network width, but does not identify a size at which the network just fits the training set or report a complete fall-rise-fall curve around that point.
No test-error sweep over training epochs is reported.
The number of training samples is not swept near an interpolation threshold.

The paper studies a particular meta-learning setup, not a broad range of model classes; its main linear-model results concern model error, and the neural-network experiment does not establish a complete classical double-descent curve.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak locations across axes.
The paper varies training-task noise and task diversity and discusses descent floors, but does not test multiple or split peaks or whether optimally tuned regularization removes them.
The results are not replotted or assessed against an effective parameter count.

rows.subject: overfitted min ℓ2-norm solution of MAML
rows.operation_detail: Analyze the high-probability model-error bound as p changes.

conditions.value: Overparameterized; αt p ≪ 1 and min{p, nt} ≫ mnv for the simplified expression

rows.measure: High-probability upper bound on model error
rows.value: The text states that the bound's bias component increases with p while its noise/task-diversity component decreases toward zero; depending on parameters, the total bound may decrease throughout or decrease and then rise to a floor.
rows.uncertainty: Theorem 1 gives probability at least 1 − η; η is defined in the theorem.
rows.locator: Sections 3.2-4, Theorem 1, Eq. (9), and discussion point 3
rows.note: This is a theoretical upper-bound result about model error, not a directly measured test-error curve.
rows.check: This is a theoretical high-probability upper bound (Eq. 9), not a measured curve. Its noise/diversity term b_ideal falls with p while its bias term rises, which also bears on V6. Fig. 2 states the bound closely matches the simulations.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2, Theorem 1, Equation (9), discussion point 3; Section 4; Appendix D.

rows.value: Figure only; text says the overall trend decreases, is not strictly monotone, and has some floors, for example at width 80.

rows.note: The authors interpret the overall decreasing trend as evidence that more parameters improve overfitted generalization. The text does not describe a peak near an interpolation threshold.
rows.check: Meta-training error is below 0.025 at all widths, so the 40–500 width range appears to lie wholly past interpolation. No interpolation threshold or peak is in range. For V1 the peak cannot be assessed; only the final fall is seen, with local floors (e.g., width 80).
